blocks.title: Machine learning
blocks.text: Machine learning lets computer systems learn patterns from data and improve with experience, without being explicitly programmed for each case, and use what they learn to make predictions or decisions.

blocks.title: Where machine learning belongs
blocks.text: The book calls machine learning a subfield of data science here, and a branch of artificial intelligence in its summary. Both views are common: machine learning is a part of artificial intelligence, and it is one of the main tools data science uses.

Machine learning analyses patterns in data to make predictions or decisions. Large datasets are used to train models, which adapt and improve as new data arrives. Instead of predefined rules, the system learns from examples; as it processes more data it becomes more accurate and efficient, powering automation and intelligent systems and reducing manual work.

Learning from data means using past information to improve decisions. Data is given to a learning model, which studies the relationships in it; repeated training reduces its errors. Learning continues, because the model is updated whenever new data is available, so the system becomes smarter over time.

In traditional programming, a programmer writes fixed rules and the program applies them to data to produce output; any change needs new code. In machine learning, the system is given data with examples of the right outputs and works out the rules (a model) itself; changes come from new data. Machine learning therefore handles complex problems better and adapts to new situations (Fig 6.3).

blocks.alt: Left panel, traditional programming: data and rules written by a programmer go into a program, which gives output; new behaviour needs new code. Right panel, machine learning: data and known outputs (examples) go into learning, which produces a model (the rules found); new behaviour comes from new data.
blocks.caption: Traditional programming and machine learning (original diagram after Fig 6.3).
blocks.long_description: A spam filter shows the difference: a programmer cannot list every spam trick as a rule, but a model trained on thousands of labelled emails finds the patterns itself.

blocks.prompt: A program converts Celsius to Fahrenheit with F = 1.8C + 32. Is this traditional programming or machine learning? How could machine learning arrive at the same rule?
blocks.explanation: Traditional programming: the rule is written by the programmer. A machine-learning model could be given many pairs of Celsius and Fahrenheit readings and, by linear regression, learn a slope of about 1.8 and an intercept of about 32.

items: Machine learning: systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
Models improve with training and new data.
Traditional: data + rules give output; ML: data + examples give the rules (a model).
